claim: Neural progenitors undergo temporal patterning to generate diverse neurons in a chronological order.
source: Neural progenitors undergo temporal patterning to generate diverse neurons in a chronological order.
evidence: This is a statement from the abstract that is supported by the broader scientific literature cited in the introduction.

claim: Temporal patterning is well-studied in the developing Drosophila brain and conserved in mammals.
source: This process is well-studied in the developing Drosophila brain and conserved in mammals.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations throughout the introduction discussing conservation across species.

claim: During larval stages, intermediate neural progenitors (INPs) serially express Dichaete (D), grainyhead (Grh) and eyeless (Ey/Pax6).
source: During larval stages, intermediate neural progenitors (INPs) serially express Dichaete (D), grainyhead (Grh) and eyeless (Ey/Pax6), but how the transitions are regulated is not precisely understood.
evidence: This is supported by prior literature cited in the manuscript (Bayraktar and Doe, 2013) and confirmed by the experimental data in this study.

claim: The study developed a method to isolate transcriptomes of INPs in their distinct temporal states.
source: Here, we developed a method to isolate transcriptomes of INPs in their distinct temporal states to identify a complete set of temporal patterning factors.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the FACS methodology and RNA sequencing described in the Results and Methods sections.

claim: The analysis identifies odd-paired (opa) as a key regulator of temporal patterning.
source: Our analysis identifies odd-paired (opa), as a key regulator of temporal patterning.
evidence: This is supported by transcriptome data showing opa expression patterns and functional experiments showing loss-of-function and gain-of-function phenotypes.

claim: Temporal patterning is initiated when the SWI/SNF complex component Osa induces D and its repressor Opa at the same time but with distinct kinetics.
source: Temporal patterning is initiated when the SWI/SNF complex component Osa induces D and its repressor Opa at the same time but with distinct kinetics.
evidence: This is supported by the sequential expression analysis of D and Opa shown in Figure 4 and the observation that both are Osa targets.

claim: High Opa levels repress D to allow Grh transcription and progress to the next temporal state.
source: Then, high Opa levels repress D to allow Grh transcription and progress to the next temporal state.
evidence: This is supported by loss-of-function experiments showing increased D+ INPs when opa is depleted, and gain-of-function experiments showing loss of D+ INPs when opa is overexpressed.

claim: Osa and its target genes opa and D form an incoherent feedforward loop (FFL).
source: We propose that Osa and its target genes opa and D form an incoherent feedforward loop (FFL) and a new mechanism allowing the successive expression of temporal identities.
evidence: This is a model proposed based on the observation that Osa activates both D and its repressor Opa, which is a characteristic of incoherent FFLs.

claim: Temporal patterning of NSCs is an evolutionary conserved process observed across species ranging from insects to mammals.
source: Importantly, temporal patterning of NSCs is an evolutionary conserved process and has been observed across species ranging from insects to mammals (Alsiö et al., 2013; Livesey and Cepko, 2001; Toma et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by the cited references.

claim: During mammalian brain development, neural progenitors in the CNS undergo temporal patterning by relying on both extrinsic as well as progenitor-intrinsic cues.
source: During mammalian brain development, neural progenitors in the central nervous system (CNS) undergo temporal patterning by relying on both extrinsic as well as progenitor-intrinsic cues.
evidence: This is supported by the examples provided in the following sentences with citations.

claim: Wnt7 is an extracellular ligand required for the switch from early to late neurogenesis in cortical progenitors.
source: Wnt7, for example, is an extracellular ligand required for the switch from early to late neurogenesis in cortical progenitors (Wang et al., 2016)
evidence: This is supported by the cited reference.

claim: Ikaros (the ortholog of the Drosophila Hunchback) is an intrinsic factor specifying early-born neuronal fates.
source: Ikaros (the ortholog of the Drosophila Hunchback), in contrast, is an intrinsic factor specifying early-born neuronal fates (Mattar et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by the cited reference.

claim: Intrinsic temporal identity factors in vertebrates are often homologous to factors described in Drosophila.
source: Like Ikaros, intrinsic temporal identity factors in vertebrates are often homologous to factors described in Drosophila (Naka et al., 2008; Ren et al., 2017; Syed et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by the cited references.

claim: During embryonic neurogenesis, Drosophila NSCs undergo temporal patterning through a cascade of transcription factors.
source: During embryonic neurogenesis, Drosophila NSCs, called Neuroblasts (NBs), undergo temporal patterning through a cascade of transcription factors (Isshiki et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by the cited reference.

claim: During larval neurogenesis, NB temporal patterning relies on opposing gradients of two RNA-binding proteins.
source: During larval neurogenesis, NB temporal patterning relies on opposing gradients of two RNA-binding proteins (Liu et al., 2015; Syed et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by the cited references.

claim: Newborn INPs undergo several maturation steps before they resume proliferation: they first turn on earmuff (erm), and Asense (ase), and finally Deadpan (Dpn) expression to become mature INPs (mINP).
source: Once they arise from an asymmetric division of a type II NB, newborn INPs undergo several maturation steps before they resume proliferation: they first turn on earmuff (erm), and Asense (ase), and finally Deadpan (Dpn) expression to become mature INPs (mINP) (Bello et al., 2008; Boone and Doe, 2008; Bowman et al., 2008; Janssens et al., 2014; Walsh and Doe, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by the cited references.

claim: Mature INPs divide 3–6 times asymmetrically to generate ganglion mother cells (GMCs), which in turn divide to generate a pair of neurons or glia.
source: Then mINPs divide 3–6 times asymmetrically to generate ganglion mother cells (GMCs), which in turn divide to generate a pair of neurons or glia.
evidence: This is established knowledge about type II NB lineages.

claim: The sequential expression of Dichaete (D), Grainyhead (Grh) and Eyeless (Ey) is required to generate different neurons.
source: Indeed, the sequential expression of Dichaete (D), Grainyhead (Grh) and Eyeless (Ey) is required to generate different neurons: D+ INPs produce Brain-specific homeobox (Bsh)+ neurons, while Ey+ INPs produce Toy+ neurons (Bayraktar and Doe, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by the cited reference and confirmed by data in this manuscript.

claim: D+ INPs produce Brain-specific homeobox (Bsh)+ neurons.
source: D+ INPs produce Brain-specific homeobox (Bsh)+ neurons, while Ey+ INPs produce Toy+ neurons (Bayraktar and Doe, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by the cited reference and confirmed by data in Figure 3.

claim: Ey+ INPs produce Toy+ neurons.
source: D+ INPs produce Brain-specific homeobox (Bsh)+ neurons, while Ey+ INPs produce Toy+ neurons (Bayraktar and Doe, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by the cited reference and confirmed by data in Figure 3.

claim: D is necessary, but not sufficient, for activating Grh.
source: D is necessary, but not sufficient, for activating Grh.
evidence: This is supported by the cited reference (Bayraktar and Doe, 2013).

claim: Grh is required for repression of D and activation of Ey.
source: Grh instead is required for repression of D and activation of Ey (Bayraktar and Doe, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by the cited reference.

claim: INP temporal patterning critically requires the SWI/SNF chromatin remodeling complex subunit Osa.
source: Intriguingly however, INP temporal patterning also critically requires the SWI/SNF chromatin remodeling complex subunit Osa (Eroglu et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by the cited reference.

claim: Osa is required to initiate temporal patterning by activating the initial factor D.
source: Although Osa is not considered a specific temporal identity factor, it is required to initiate temporal patterning by activating the initial factor D.
evidence: This is supported by the cited reference (Eroglu et al., 2014).

claim: The Osa target gene hamlet is required for the Grh-to-Ey transition.
source: While the Osa target gene hamlet is required for the Grh-to-Ey transition (Eroglu et al., 2014), regulation of the first transition is less well understood.
evidence: This is supported by the cited reference.

claim: D and ham double knock down phenotypes do not recapitulate the complete loss of temporal patterning initiation observed in Osa-depleted type II NB lineages.
source: Nevertheless, D and ham double knock down (k.d.) phenotypes do not recapitulate the complete loss of temporal patterning initiation observed in Osa-depleted type II NB lineages, suggesting the contribution of additional unidentified factors.
evidence: This is an observation from prior work that motivates the current study.

claim: The study used FACS to purify INPs at each of their three temporal states: D+, Grh+ and Ey+.
source: To obtain a comprehensive list of temporally regulated genes in INPs, we used FACS to purify INPs at each of their three temporal states: D+, Grh+ and Ey+ (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the methodology described and shown in Figure 1.

claim: Fly lines were generated expressing tdTomato under an INP specific promoter (erm-Gal4 >CD8::tdTomato) and expressing GFP-fusions of one of the temporal identity factors (D-GFP, Grh-GFP and Ey-GFP).
source: For this, we generated fly lines expressing tdTomato under an INP specific promoter (erm-Gal4 >CD8::tdTomato) and expressing GFP-fusions of one of the temporal identity factors (D-GFP, Grh-GFP and Ey-GFP, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is described in the methods and shown in supplementary figures.

claim: D-GFP flies were generated with CRISPR/Cas9 method to knock-in GFP into the endogenous locus.
source: Although D-GFP flies were generated with CRISPR/Cas9 method to knock-in GFP into the endogenous locus, Grh-GFP and Ey-GFP flies were generated as BAC clones insertions (Spokony and White, 2012).
evidence: This is described in the methods section.

claim: Grh-GFP and Ey-GFP flies were generated as BAC clones insertions.
source: Although D-GFP flies were generated with CRISPR/Cas9 method to knock-in GFP into the endogenous locus, Grh-GFP and Ey-GFP flies were generated as BAC clones insertions (Spokony and White, 2012).
evidence: This is described in the methods section with citation.

claim: All sorted cells within the INP populations expressed Dpn, indicating a 100% mature INP identity.
source: All sorted cells within the INP populations expressed Dpn, indicating a 100% mature INP identity, while unsorted cells showed a mixture of Dpn+ and Dpn- cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C-D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C-D.

claim: Each GFP+ sorted INP population was 100% positive for its respective temporal marker.
source: Importantly, each GFP+ sorted INP population was 100% positive for its respective temporal marker (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1F quantification.

claim: Sorted populations contained only 4–6% of double-positive cells expressing markers of two temporal identities.
source: Analyzing Grh IF on D-GFP+ and Ey-GFP+ sorted cells, and Ey IF on Grh-GFP+ sorted cells revealed that sorted populations contained only 4–6% of such double-positive cells (Figure 1C–F, and Figure 1—figure supplement 2A-C), suggesting we can isolate almost pure populations of different temporal states.
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunofluorescence analysis shown in the cited figures.

claim: 458 genes were found expressed differently between D+ and Grh+ INPs.
source: With this RNA sequencing strategy, we found 458 genes expressed differently between D+ and Grh+ INPs, and 466 genes between Grh+ and Ey+ INPs (FDR 0.05, log2foldchange > 1, and Rpm (reads per million mapped reads)>10 in one of three samples/D+, Grh+ or Ey+ INPs).
evidence: This is from the RNA sequencing analysis described in the Results.

claim: 466 genes were found expressed differently between Grh+ and Ey+ INPs.
source: With this RNA sequencing strategy, we found 458 genes expressed differently between D+ and Grh+ INPs, and 466 genes between Grh+ and Ey+ INPs (FDR 0.05, log2foldchange > 1, and Rpm (reads per million mapped reads)>10 in one of three samples/D+, Grh+ or Ey+ INPs).
evidence: This is from the RNA sequencing analysis described in the Results.

claim: FACS-purified Grh+ INPs expressed high levels of Ey mRNA.
source: FACS-purified Grh+ INPs expressed high levels of Ey mRNA.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1F.

claim: Grh+ INPs expressed only low levels of Ey protein.
source: However, immunofluorescent analysis showed that Grh+ INPs expressed only low levels of Ey protein, suggesting that post-transcriptional modifications regulate the Grh-to-Ey transition (Figure 1C–F and Figure 1—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunofluorescence data in the cited figures.

claim: Post-transcriptional modifications regulate the Grh-to-Ey transition.
source: However, immunofluorescent analysis showed that Grh+ INPs expressed only low levels of Ey protein, suggesting that post-transcriptional modifications regulate the Grh-to-Ey transition (Figure 1C–F and Figure 1—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This is inferred from the discrepancy between mRNA and protein levels.

claim: Genes upregulated in D+ INPs showed enrichment for mitochondrial translation, cellular nitrogen compound metabolic process and gene expression.
source: Genes upregulated in D+ INPs showed enrichment for mitochondrial translation, cellular nitrogen compound metabolic process and gene expression (Figure 1—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: This is from GO-term analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2D.

claim: Genes upregulated in Grh +INPs were enriched for protein binding and system development.
source: Genes upregulated in Grh +INPs were enriched for protein binding and system development (Figure 1—figure supplement 2E).
evidence: This is from GO-term analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2E.

claim: Genes upregulated in Ey +INPs were enriched for neurogenesis and sequence-specific DNA binding.
source: Finally, genes upregulated in Ey +INPs were enriched for neurogenesis and sequence-specific DNA binding (Figure 1—figure supplement 2F).
evidence: This is from GO-term analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2F.

claim: The glial identity-promoting factor glial cell missing (gcm) was upregulated in Ey+ INPs.
source: Interestingly, we observed that the glial identity-promoting factor glial cell missing (gcm) and cell cycle inhibitor dacapo (dap) were upregulated in Ey+ INPs (Figure 1G—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This is shown in the RNA sequencing data.

claim: Cell cycle inhibitor dacapo (dap) was upregulated in Ey+ INPs.
source: Interestingly, we observed that the glial identity-promoting factor glial cell missing (gcm) and cell cycle inhibitor dacapo (dap) were upregulated in Ey+ INPs (Figure 1G—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This is shown in the RNA sequencing data.

claim: INPs begin producing glia cells instead of neurons during their later cell divisions.
source: These observations support previous findings indicating that INPs begin producing glia cells instead of neurons during their later cell divisions, and that Ey is required for cell cycle exit (Baumgardt et al., 2014; Bayraktar and Doe, 2013; Ren et al., 2018; Viktorin et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by the cited references and the observation of gcm upregulation in Ey+ INPs.

claim: Ey is required for cell cycle exit.
source: These observations support previous findings indicating that INPs begin producing glia cells instead of neurons during their later cell divisions, and that Ey is required for cell cycle exit (Baumgardt et al., 2014; Bayraktar and Doe, 2013; Ren et al., 2018; Viktorin et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by the cited references and the observation of dap upregulation in Ey+ INPs.

claim: 71 genes were identified with dynamic expression patterns between INP populations using specific filtering criteria.
source: We applied a cut-off of Rpm (reads per million mapped reads)>50 in one of the three temporal identity states due to the fact that all the other temporal identity factors, along with osa and ham, had high expression levels. With these criteria, we identified 71 genes (Supplementary file 1 and Supplementary file 2)
evidence: This is from the RNA sequencing analysis with specific filtering criteria applied.

claim: 49 genes displayed an expression pattern of high in D + INPs, low in Grh +INPs, and finally higher in Ey +INPs.
source: 49 of which displayed an expression pattern of high in D + INPs, low in Grh +INPs, and finally higher in Ey +INPs.
evidence: This is from the RNA sequencing analysis.

claim: Odd-paired (opa) was ranked as the 5th hit that is most downregulated in Grh+ INPs.
source: Among these genes, odd-paired (opa) was ranked as the 5th hit that is most downregulated in Grh+ INPs (Figure 1G–I, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is from the RNA sequencing analysis shown in Figure 1G-I.

claim: Osa binds to the TSS of opa in order to prime its expression.
source: Since Osa binds to the TSS of opa in order to prime its expression (Eroglu et al., 2014), we investigated in detail the potential role of Opa in regulating INP temporal patterning.
evidence: This is supported by the cited reference.

claim: Opa is a transcription factor containing five zinc finger domains.
source: Opa is a transcription factor containing five zinc finger domains and is essential for para-segmental subdivision of Drosophila embryos (Benedyk et al., 1994; Mizugishi et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by the cited references.

claim: Opa is essential for para-segmental subdivision of Drosophila embryos.
source: Opa is a transcription factor containing five zinc finger domains and is essential for para-segmental subdivision of Drosophila embryos (Benedyk et al., 1994; Mizugishi et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by the cited references.

claim: During development, Opa ensures the timely activation of the transcription factors engrailed and wingless.
source: During development, Opa ensures the timely activation of the transcription factors engrailed and wingless (Benedyk et al., 1994).
evidence: This is supported by the cited reference.

claim: Opa knockdown slightly increased the total number of INPs (Dpn+ cells).
source: Opa knockdown slightly increased the total number of INPs (Dpn+ cells), but drastically increased the number of D+ INPs while decreasing the number of both Grh+ and Ey+ INPs (Figure 2A–D).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2A-D with quantification.

claim: Opa knockdown drastically increased the number of D+ INPs while decreasing the number of both Grh+ and Ey+ INPs.
source: Opa knockdown slightly increased the total number of INPs (Dpn+ cells), but drastically increased the number of D+ INPs while decreasing the number of both Grh+ and Ey+ INPs (Figure 2A–D).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2A-D with quantification.

claim: Opa mutant clones contained predominantly D+ INPs, at the expense of the other two temporal states.
source: Control clones were indistinguishable from WT, whereas opa mutant clones contained predominantly D+ INPs, at the expense of the other two temporal states (Figure 2E–F).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2E-F using MARCM analysis.

claim: Loss of Opa causes a shift in INP temporal state identity such that the early generated D+ INPs are increased while the later generated Grh+ and Ey+ INPs are decreased.
source: The RNAi and mosaic mutant analysis both indicate that loss of Opa causes a shift in INP temporal state identity such that the early generated D+ INPs are increased while the later generated Grh+ and Ey+ INPs are decreased.
evidence: This is inferred from the RNAi and MARCM data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Opa is regulating the D-to-Grh transition by either repressing D or activating Grh.
source: These results suggest that opa is regulating the D-to-Grh transition by either repressing D or activating Grh.
evidence: This is inferred from the loss-of-function phenotypes.

claim: Grh is not sufficient for D repression.
source: Since it has been previously shown that Grh is not sufficient for D repression (Bayraktar and Doe, 2013), we tested whether the main role of opa is to repress D.
evidence: This is supported by the cited reference.

claim: Opa knock-down in DM1 lineages caused a significant increase in the number of D+ INPs at the expense of Ey+ INPs.
source: Opa knock-down in DM1 lineages caused a significant increase in the number of D+ INPs at the expense of Ey+ INPs, suggesting that opa is required for D repression (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Opa is required for D repression.
source: Opa knock-down in DM1 lineages caused a significant increase in the number of D+ INPs at the expense of Ey+ INPs, suggesting that opa is required for D repression (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is inferred from the DM1 lineage experiments.

claim: INP-driven opa RNAi displayed a significant increase in Bsh+ neurons, at the expense of Toy+ neurons.
source: INP-driven opa RNAi displayed a significant increase in Bsh+ neurons, at the expense of Toy+ neurons (Figure 3A–C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3A-C with quantification.

claim: Opa-depleted MARCM clones contained increased numbers of Bsh+ neurons compared to wild-type counterparts.
source: In addition, opa-depleted MARCM clones also contained increased numbers of Bsh+ neurons compared to wild-type counterparts (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Shifting the INP identity toward a D+ identity leads to a concomitant increase in the Bsh+ neurons produced by D+ INPs.
source: This result confirms that shifting the INP identity toward a D+ identity leads to a concomitant increase in the Bsh+ neurons produced by D+ INPs.
evidence: This is inferred from the neuronal marker analysis in opa loss-of-function experiments.

claim: Altering the temporal identity progression of neural progenitors can alter the proportions of neuronal subtypes in the brain.
source: Thus, altering the temporal identity progression of neural progenitors can alter the proportions of neuronal subtypes in the brain.
evidence: This is concluded from the observation that opa depletion changes both INP temporal identity and neuronal subtype proportions.

claim: The adult central complex (CCX) brain region relies on type II NB neurogenesis.
source: The adult central complex (CCX) brain region relies on type II NB neurogenesis (Bayraktar et al., 2010; Izergina et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by the cited references.

claim: Opa-depletion in INPs caused major alterations in the gross morphology of the adult CCX.
source: Opa-depletion in INPs caused major alterations in the gross morphology of the adult CCX. The fan-shaped body (FB) was enlarged, the noduli (NO) and ellipsoid body (EB) only partially formed, and the protocerebral bridge (PB) appeared fragmented (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3E.

claim: The CCX is required for adult motor functions.
source: Since the CCX is required for adult motor functions (Callaerts et al., 2001; Young and Armstrong, 2010), we tested whether altered CCX morphology affected motor behavior.
evidence: This is supported by the cited references.

claim: INP-driven opa RNAi caused impaired negative geotaxis performance.
source: Compared to control flies, INP-driven opa RNAi caused impaired negative geotaxis performance (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3F with quantification.

claim: Opa is a temporal switch gene required for neuronal subtype specification.
source: Thus, opa is a temporal switch gene required for neuronal subtype specification, which is required for the correct assembly and function of the adult central complex.
evidence: This is concluded from the combined observations of temporal identity defects, neuronal subtype changes, and behavioral deficits.

claim: The temporal identity specification of neural progenitors is crucial for proper neural cell complexity, and brain function.
source: Thus, the temporal identity specification of neural progenitors is crucial for proper neural cell complexity, and brain function.
evidence: This is concluded from the observation that disrupting temporal patterning affects brain structure and behavior.

claim: Opa is expressed throughout the type II lineage in INPs and GMCs and neurons, but not in NBs or immature INPs.
source: Through immunofluorescent analysis of V5 tag expression, we observed that Opa is expressed throughout the type II lineage in INPs (marked with Dpn and Ase) and, GMCs (Pros+ cells) and neurons, but not in NBs (Dpn+) or immature INPs (Dpn-/Ase- or Dpn-/Ase+ cells) (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B-D).
evidence: This is shown by immunofluorescence analysis in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B-D.

claim: Opa is also expressed in the DM1 lineage.
source: Opa is also expressed in the DM1 lineage, even though DM1 lineages display a temporal patterning lacking Grh expression (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1E.

claim: The proper expression of opa is dependent on Osa.
source: The proper expression of opa is dependent on Osa, since Osa-knockdown in type II NBs resulted in a loss of Opa (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A and B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2A and B.

claim: D+/opa- INPs appeared before D+/opa+ cells in the lineage.
source: Without exception, D+/opa- INPs appeared before D+/opa+ cells in the lineage (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4A.

claim: All Grh+ and Ey+ INPs expressed opa.
source: However, in later temporal states, all Grh+ and Ey+ INPs expressed opa (Figure 4B, and Figure 4—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 3A.

claim: D+ INPs express the highest opa protein levels.
source: Indeed, we found that D+ INPs express the highest opa protein levels (Figure 4C)
evidence: This is shown by intensity measurements in Figure 4C.

claim: Grh+ INPs express the lowest opa protein levels.
source: while Grh+ INPs express the lowest (Figure 4D and Figure 4—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: This is shown by intensity measurements in Figure 4D and Figure 4—figure supplement 3B.

claim: D knockdown alone did not prevent later temporal stages, Grh and Ey, to appear.
source: Interestingly, D knockdown alone also did not prevent later temporal stages, Grh and Ey, to appear (Bayraktar and Doe, 2013), suggesting that other factor(s) are required to maintain temporal identities in INPs.
evidence: This is supported by the cited reference.

claim: Double knock down of D and opa by type II NB-specific RNAi produced type II lineages containing fewer Dpn+/Ase+ INPs compared to controls.
source: Double knock down of D and opa by type II NB-specific RNAi produced type II lineages containing fewer Dpn+/Ase+ INPs compared to controls (Figure 4F–G).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4F-G.

claim: All known temporal identity markers on the remaining cells were absent in D and opa double knockdown, suggesting a complete loss of temporal identity in these INPs.
source: Importantly, all known temporal identity markers on the remaining cells were absent, suggesting a complete loss of temporal identity in these INPs (Figure 4F–G).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4F-G.

claim: Opa is required for the repression of D, the activation of Grh, and thus the progression of temporal identities in INPs.
source: Therefore, our data suggest that opa is required for the repression of D, the activation of Grh, and thus the progression of temporal identities in INPs.
evidence: This is concluded from the combined loss-of-function and epistasis experiments.

claim: Overexpression of opa resulted in shorter lineages.
source: Overexpression of opa resulted in shorter lineages (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A-B), decreased total INP numbers (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A), and a loss of type II NBs (marked by Dpn or Mira) (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A-B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A-B.

claim: Overexpression of opa resulted in decreased total INP numbers.
source: Overexpression of opa resulted in shorter lineages (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A-B), decreased total INP numbers (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A), and a loss of type II NBs (marked by Dpn or Mira) (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A-B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Overexpression of opa resulted in a loss of type II NBs.
source: Overexpression of opa resulted in shorter lineages (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A-B), decreased total INP numbers (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A), and a loss of type II NBs (marked by Dpn or Mira) (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A-B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A-B.

claim: Co-expressing the apoptosis inhibitor p35 did not prevent NB loss or shortened lineages upon opa overexpression.
source: Co-expressing the apoptosis inhibitor p35 did not prevent NB loss or shortened lineages, suggesting that opa overexpression does not induce cell death, but causes premature differentiation instead (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Opa overexpression does not induce cell death, but causes premature differentiation.
source: Co-expressing the apoptosis inhibitor p35 did not prevent NB loss or shortened lineages, suggesting that opa overexpression does not induce cell death, but causes premature differentiation instead (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is inferred from the p35 rescue experiment.

claim: Overexpressing opa in type II NB lineages caused complete loss of D+ INPs.
source: Overexpressing opa in type II NB lineages caused complete loss of D+ INPs, but the few remaining INPs could still activate Grh and Ey (Figure 5A–C)
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5A-C with quantification.

claim: The few remaining INPs upon opa overexpression in type II NBs could still activate Grh and Ey.
source: Overexpressing opa in type II NB lineages caused complete loss of D+ INPs, but the few remaining INPs could still activate Grh and Ey (Figure 5A–C)
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5A-C.

claim: Opa overexpression in an INP-specific manner caused a decrease in D+ INPs.
source: Opa overexpression caused a decrease in D+ INPs (Figure 5D–F), and a concomitant increase in both Grh+ and Ey+ INP populations (Figure 5D–F).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5D-F with quantification.

claim: Opa overexpression in an INP-specific manner caused a concomitant increase in both Grh+ and Ey+ INP populations.
source: Opa overexpression caused a decrease in D+ INPs (Figure 5D–F), and a concomitant increase in both Grh+ and Ey+ INP populations (Figure 5D–F).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5D-F with quantification.

claim: Opa represses the early D+ temporal identity, but also activates later Grh+ temporal identity.
source: This result further indicates that Opa represses the early D+ temporal identity, but also activates later Grh+ temporal identity.
evidence: This is inferred from the gain-of-function experiments.

claim: Opa overexpression in DM1 lineages resulted in a decrease in D+ INP numbers and an increase in Ey+ INPs.
source: We also overexpressed opa in DM1 lineages in an INP-specific manner, which resulted in a decrease in D+ INP numbers and an increase in Ey+ INPs (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A and C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2A and C.

claim: Opa mis-expression does not cause ectopic Grh expression in DM1 lineages.
source: However, ectopic Grh expression was undetectable (Figure 5—figure supplement 2B), suggesting opa mis-expression does not cause ectopic Grh expression.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Opa-mediated repression of D depends on Opa expression levels.
source: Collectively, these results show that opa-mediated repression of D depends on Opa expression levels.
evidence: This is concluded from the observation that D+/opa+ cells exist, but high opa levels repress D.

claim: Co-expressing opa RNAi with ham shmiR in an INP-specific manner caused supernumerary Dpn+, Ase+ INPs.
source: Co-expressing opa RNAi with ham shmiR in an INP-specific manner caused supernumerary Dpn+, Ase+ INPs (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The number of D+/Dpn+ and Grh+/Dpn+ INPs were increased in opa and ham double knockdown.
source: In addition, the number of D+/Dpn+ and Grh+/Dpn+ INPs were also increased, which is in contrast to single depletion of opa or ham (Figure 6A–B, Figure 2; Eroglu et al., 2014).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6A-B.

claim: Opa and ham loss-of-function phenotypes are additive.
source: Thus, opa and ham loss-of-function phenotypes are additive.
evidence: This is concluded from the double knockdown experiments.

claim: Depleting both opa and ham in type II NBs could not recapitulate the Osa loss-of-function phenotype because imINPs could mature and express Ase.
source: Importantly, despite inducing over-proliferation of mature INPs (Ase+/Dpn+), depleting both opa and ham in type II NBs could not recapitulate the Osa loss-of-function phenotype because imINPs could mature and express Ase, and therefore did not revert into ectopic NBs (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Osa regulates temporal patterning in two levels: initiation by D activation, and progression by opa and ham.
source: This suggests that Osa regulates temporal patterning in two levels: initiation by D activation, and progression by opa and ham.
evidence: This is concluded from the comparison of Osa, D, opa, and ham phenotypes.

claim: Osa initiates temporal patterning by activating the transcription factor D.
source: Initially, Osa initiates temporal patterning by activating the transcription factor D.
evidence: This is supported by prior work (Eroglu et al., 2014) and the current study.

claim: Osa regulates the progression of temporal patterning by activating opa and ham, which in turn downregulate D and Grh, respectively.
source: Subsequently, Osa regulates the progression of temporal patterning by activating opa and ham, which in turn downregulate D and Grh, respectively (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is the model proposed based on the experimental data.

claim: Opa regulates the transition from D to Grh.
source: For instance, opa regulates the transition from D to Grh, while ham regulates the transition from Grh to Ey.
evidence: This is concluded from the loss-of-function phenotypes.

claim: Ham regulates the transition from Grh to Ey.
source: For instance, opa regulates the transition from D to Grh, while ham regulates the transition from Grh to Ey.
evidence: This is supported by prior work (Eroglu et al., 2014).

claim: Opa achieves temporal transition by repressing D and activating grh.
source: We propose that opa achieves this by repressing D and activating grh, as indicated by the lack of temporal patterning in D and opa-depleted INPs (Figure 4C–D, Figure 6C).
evidence: This is proposed based on the double knockdown experiments.

claim: D and opa activate Grh expression against the presence of ham, which represses Grh expression.
source: Moreover, we propose that D and opa activate Grh expression against the presence of ham, which represses Grh expression.
evidence: This is a model proposed to explain how temporal transitions are regulated.

claim: As D and opa levels decrease as INPs age and become Grh positive, ham is capable of repressing Grh later on in temporal patterning.
source: As D and opa levels decrease as INPs age and become Grh positive, ham is capable of repressing Grh later on in temporal patterning (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is a model proposed to explain the temporal dynamics.

claim: Opa and ham act only during specific stages even though they are expressed throughout the entire lineage.
source: This explains how opa and ham act only during specific stages even though they are expressed throughout the entire lineage.
evidence: This is inferred from the expression patterns and functional data.

claim: The double knock-down of opa and ham failed to recapitulate the Osa phenotype.
source: An open question pertains to the fact that the double knock-down of opa and ham, as well as that of D and opa, failed to recapitulate the Osa phenotype.
evidence: This is observed in the experiments shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The initiation of the first temporal identity state may block the reversion of INPs to a NB-state.
source: Thus, the initiation of the first temporal identity state may block the reversion of INPs to a NB-state.
evidence: This is proposed to explain why opa/ham double knockdown doesn't produce ectopic NBs like Osa knockdown does.

claim: Osa initiates D expression earlier than opa expression.
source: We further demonstrate that Osa initiates D expression earlier than opa expression.
evidence: This is shown by the sequential expression analysis in Figure 4A.

claim: Osa is a subunit of SWI/SNF chromatin remodeling complex, and it guides the complex to specific loci throughout the genome, such as the TSS of both D and opa.
source: Osa is a subunit of SWI/SNF chromatin remodeling complex, and it guides the complex to specific loci throughout the genome, such as the TSS of both D and opa.
evidence: This is supported by prior work (Eroglu et al., 2014) showing Osa binding to these loci.

claim: The transcription factor earmuff may activate D.
source: Previous work suggests that the transcription factor earmuff may activate (Janssens et al., 2014; Janssens et al., 2017).
evidence: This is suggested by the cited references.

claim: It remains unknown which factor activates opa expression.
source: However, it remains unknown which factor activates opa expression.
evidence: This is stated as an open question.

claim: The cell cycle may activate opa, since its expression begins in mINPs, a dividing cell unlike imINPs, which are in cell cycle arrest.
source: One possibility is that the cell cycle activates opa, since its expression begins in mINPs, a dividing cell unlike imINPs, which are in cell cycle arrest.
evidence: This is speculation based on the correlation between opa expression and cell cycle state.

claim: Balanced expression levels of D and opa regulates the timing of transitions between temporal identity states.
source: We propose that balanced expression levels of D and opa regulates the timing of transitions between temporal identity states.
evidence: This is proposed based on the observation that opa levels affect D expression.

claim: Osa initiates D and opa at slightly different times, which could allow a time window for D to be expressed, perform its function, then become repressed again by opa.
source: Indeed, Osa initiates D and opa, the repressor of D, at slightly different times, which could allow a time window for D to be expressed, perform its function, then become repressed again by opa.
evidence: This is proposed based on the sequential expression data.

claim: Deregulating the balanced expression of D and opa, for example by overexpressing opa in the earliest INP stage, results in a false start of temporal patterning and premature differentiation.
source: Deregulating this pattern, for example by overexpressing opa in the earliest INP stage, results in a false start of temporal patterning and premature differentiation.
evidence: This is observed in the opa overexpression experiments.

claim: This set of genetic interactions resembles that of an incoherent feedforward loop (FFL).
source: This elegant set of genetic interactions resembles that of an incoherent feedforward loop (FFL) (Kim et al., 2008; Mangan and Alon, 2003).
evidence: This is a comparison to a known network motif with citations.

claim: In an incoherent FFL, an upstream gene directly activates the target gene, meanwhile indirectly repressing it by activating its repressor.
source: In such a network, pathways have opposing roles. For instance, Osa promotes both the expression and repression of D.
evidence: This is the definition of an incoherent FFL applied to the Osa-D-opa system.

claim: In the galactose network of E. coli, the transcriptional activator CRP activates galS and galE, while galS also represses galE.
source: Similar examples can be observed in other organisms, such as in the galactose network of E. coli, where the transcriptional activator CRP activates galS and galE, while galS also represses galE (Shen-Orr et al., 2002).
evidence: This is an example from the literature cited.

claim: In Drosophila SOP determination, miR-7, together with Atonal forms an incoherent FFL.
source: In Drosophila SOP determination, miR-7, together with Atonal also forms an incoherent FFL (Li et al., 2009).
evidence: This is an example from the literature cited.

claim: Mammals apply a similar mechanism in the c-Myc/E2F1 regulatory system.
source: Furthermore, mammals apply a similar mechanism in the c-Myc/E2F1 regulatory system (O'Donnell et al., 2005).
evidence: This is an example from the literature cited.

claim: The vertebrate homologues of opa consist of the Zinc-finger protein of the cerebellum (ZIC) family.
source: The vertebrate homologues of opa consist of the Zinc-finger protein of the cerebellum (ZIC) family, which are suggested to regulate the transcriptional activity of target genes, and to have a role in CNS development (Elms et al., 2004; Elms et al., 2003; Gaston-Massuet et al., 2005; Inoue et al., 2004; Inoue et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by the cited references.

claim: ZIC family proteins are suggested to regulate the transcriptional activity of target genes, and to have a role in CNS development.
source: The vertebrate homologues of opa consist of the Zinc-finger protein of the cerebellum (ZIC) family, which are suggested to regulate the transcriptional activity of target genes, and to have a role in CNS development (Elms et al., 2004; Elms et al., 2003; Gaston-Massuet et al., 2005; Inoue et al., 2004; Inoue et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by the cited references.

claim: In mice, during embryonic cortical development, ZIC family proteins regulate the proliferation of meningeal cells, which are required for normal cortical development.
source: In mice, during embryonic cortical development, ZIC family proteins regulate the proliferation of meningeal cells, which are required for normal cortical development (Inoue et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by the cited reference.

claim: Zic1 is a Brn2 target, which itself controls the transition from early-to-mid neurogenesis in the mouse cortex.
source: In addition, another member of the ZIC family, Zic1, is a Brn2 target, which itself controls the transition from early-to-mid neurogenesis in the mouse cortex (Urban et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by the cited reference.

claim: ZIC family is important in brain development in zebrafish.
source: Along with these lines, it has been shown that ZIC family is important in brain development in zebrafish (Maurus and Harris, 2009; Sanek and Grinblat, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by the cited references.

claim: The role of ZIC has been implicated in variety of brain malformations and/or diseases.
source: Furthermore, the role of ZIC has been implicated in variety of brain malformations and/or diseases (Aruga et al., 2010; Blank et al., 2011; Hatayama et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by the cited references.

claim: Temporal patterning is a highly coordinated ensemble that allows regulation on additional levels than was previously appreciated to ensure a perfectly balanced generation of different neuron/glial cell types.
source: In contrast to existing cascade models, we instead show that temporal patterning is a highly coordinated ensemble that allows regulation on additional levels than was previously appreciated to ensure a perfectly balanced generation of different neuron/glial cell types.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study.

claim: Drosophila is a powerful system to dissect the genetic mechanisms underlying the temporal patterning of neural stem cells and how the disruption of such mechanisms impacts brain development and behavior.
source: Together, our results demonstrate that Drosophila is a powerful system to dissect the genetic mechanisms underlying the temporal patterning of neural stem cells and how the disruption of such mechanisms impacts brain development and behavior.
evidence: This is a concluding statement supported by the entire study.
